title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) agents can use external tools to help users solve complex tasks. However, for problems that require learning from long-term historical events or from previous agent-environment interactions, LLM agents are required to use memory mechanisms to store and retrieve experiences. While sophisticated memory systems exist for dialogue agents, few studies have empirically examined how to improve agents' tool-using capabilities through past user-agent conversations. We propose MemToolAgent, a framework that improves tool use through memory management. Our approach contains a memory extraction module that processes past experiences into structured memory entries, and a retrieval module that dynamically selects a subset of the stored memory entries. This enables more personalized and accurate responses aligned with user preferences and feedback without requiring LLM fine-tuning. In summary, this work has three main contributions: (1) a unified memory entry format that improves both general-purpose and personalized tool use without LLM fine-tuning, (2) a reflection-based memory extraction that uses environment and user feedback to distill wrong executions into critiques to store, and (3) a retrieval module that chooses how many past experiences to use based on the memory similarity distribution. MemToolAgent achieves 29%, 80%, and 17% relative improvements compared to strong baselines on the WorkBench, NESTFUL, and PEToolBench benchmarks, respectively.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Combining powerful LLMs with additional components like memory systems, workflow mechanisms, APIs, and other tools to create LLM agents is an emerging trend. These agents are designed to solve complex tasks that require sequential reasoning and multi-step planning. In this context, tools are functions utilized by agents to interact with their environment. Integrating LLMs with external tools and APIs allows these language models to leverage various systems, enabling end-users to interact with those systems through a chat interface. An LLM agent's tool use ability, i.e., using appropriate tools for solving a task, is an important capability.

Despite significant advancements in recent years, fixed context windows of LLMs limit maintaining coherence and thematic continuity during long realworld conversations (Tan et al., 2025). Due to long sequences containing abundant irrelevant information, the attention mechanism loses its effectiveness, which is not desired for critical scenarios in education and healthcare. As a result, integrating memory mechanisms into agents is crucial for long-term interaction ability. LLM agents need reliable external feedback to correct themselves (Kamoi et al., 2024), and memory can provide this feedback by storing and retrieving past interactions. Using experiences allows agents to more accurately anticipate user needs and learn from mistakes.

Integrating memory into an LLM agent supports two main types of tasks: personalized and generalpurpose tool use, as shown in Figure 1. Users utilize the same tools in particular ways, such as using different input parameters, or they might use different tools to achieve the same goal. In scenarios where the agent has access to tools with similar functionalities, it requires user context to correctly execute the task. Storing the past interactions in the memory allows for better personalization. For instance, personalization can resolve the tool-level ambiguity if "create a ticket" could refer to Zendesk ticket creation or Jira issue creation. Regarding general-purpose tool use, there are common error patterns in tool use agents, such as dependency violation, parameter hallucination, and premature tool calling. Having past experiences in memory can help the agent use the correct parameters for tools and use the tools in the correct order. For example, this is useful in scenarios where the agent utilizes the same set of tools for a group of users to solve generic tasks like forwarding emails.

Our work offers three main contributions: (1) a unified memory entry format of storing past experiences for better general-purpose and personalized tool use performance without LLM fine-tuning, (2) an environment and user feedback-based reflection approach for memory writing to distill failed past experiences into critiques, and (3) a retrieval module based on similarity distribution that dynamically selects relevant memory entries to guide the agent for the current task.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.text:
There has been a growing interest in memory management for LLM agents in recent years. A related earlier idea is Case-based reasoning (CBR) (Aamodt and Plaza, 1994) where systems retrieve and use similar past cases (experiences) to solve new problems. MemGPT (MemoryGPT) (Packer et al., 2023) introduces an OS-inspired memory hierarchy with two memory types called the main context and the external context. More recent work includes graph-based architectures to organize the information more flexibly and expressively. In Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), the memory is modeled as a directed knowledge graph to express complex relationships. This allows dynamic and more advanced storage and retrieval. A-MEM (Agentic Memory) (Xu et al., 2025b) proposes a memory based on the Zettelkasten knowledge management system. The memory entries are linked as interconnected networks, and the existing entries are updated based on new experiences. Similarly, Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025) and Cognitive Weave (Vishwakarma et al., 2025) are based on temporally aware knowledge graphs and Spatio-Temporal Resonance Graphs, respectively.

Reflexion agents (Shinn et al., 2023) turn task feedback into self-reflections that are stored in an episodic memory for subsequent runs. Reflective Memory Management (RMM) (Tan et al., 2025) uses a Reinforcement Learning based approach to rank memory entries based on their utilities in past executions. PersonaAgent (Zhang et al., 2025a) combines episodic and semantic memory for an LLM agent with personalized memory that enables the agent to perform actions customized to the user. Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024b) stores workflows in the memory to guide the agent in web navigation tasks. EXPEREPAIR (Mu et al., 2025) introduces an agent with a dual-memory mechanism for code repair. T1 (Chakraborty et al., 2025) uses a simple cache for agents to store tool call results. However, the main goal is to reuse the previously accessed data.

M em p (Fang et al., 2025) is a procedural memory framework that extracts both fine-grained instructions and high-level abstractions from past agent trajectories. Memento (Zhou et al., 2025) stores past experiences in an episodic memory, learns and continually updates a case-selection policy based on environmental feedback. Training-Free GRPO (Cai et al., 2025) is a training-free alternative to agentic RL that optimizes an experience library consisting of natural-language experiential knowledge. TOOLMEM (Xiao et al., 2025) stores memories of tool capabilities from previous interactions and helps the agent select the most suitable tool for a given task at inference. LEGOMem (Han et al., 2025) is a procedural memory approach for multi-agent systems that distills only success-Figure 2: MemToolAgent overview with a simple restaurant booking scenario where the agent retrieves similar memories, receives feedback on an invalid time format, and generates a reflection to update its memory ful task trajectories into memory entries with brief reflections. ReMem agents (Wei et al., 2025) combine reasoning, action, and memory refinement and actively exploit, prune, and reorganize their memory while solving the current task.

There are in-context learning (ICL) approaches closely related to agents with memory. For example, STE (Wang et al., 2024a) creates tool use trajectories based on a trial-and-error approach offline and stores them in a static memory for inference. In-Context Abstraction Learning (ICAL) (Sarch et al., 2024) creates memory abstractions from suboptimal trajectories based on human-in-the-loop learning and self-reflection.

Unlike the related work, MemToolAgent addresses both personalized and general-purpose tool use. It proposes a general memory entry format and stores and leverages detailed information like tool trajectories and a reflection/critique about the execution. Importantly, MemToolAgent also incorporates user feedback as a signal to improve the quality of memory entries.

sections.heading: Method: MemToolAgent
sections.text:
MemToolAgent consists of two main components: the memory retrieval and memory extraction modules. Figure 2 illustrates the general overview of our proposed approach. Memory entries, i.e., past experiences, are retrieved from the memory based on the semantic similarity between the query and the entries. Dynamic "n" Top-n Embedding-based Retrieval is proposed for retrieval. Instead of retrieving a fixed number of memory entries for each query, the number of entries to retrieve is dynamically determined based on the cosine similarities between the embeddings of memory entries' queries and the test query. Then, the entries are used as incontext learning to guide the agent for the current task.

To add a new entry to the memory based on the current query, an LLM-based "Memory Extraction" module provides a reflection/critique of the execution, which is then stored in the memory with the query and user feedback.

MemToolAgent specifies what to store in memory with a general memory entry format. Each memory entry m is represented as a tuple m = (q, a, f, r) where:

• q: the user query • a = {a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a n }: the sequence of tool calls executed by the agent

• f ∈ {0, 1}: binary user feedback indicating task success (f = 1) or failure (f = 0)

• r: reflection or critique generated by the memory extractor when f = 0 (otherwise r = ∅)

With binary user feedback, we simulate the scenarios where the user does not know anything about the underlying tools/APIs and gives feedback based on the outcome. However, this feedback could easily be replaced by any other type of feedback, such as text or score. Figure 3 illustrates an example memory entry with reflection.

sections.heading: Memory Retrieval: Dynamic "n" Top-n
sections.text:
Embedding-based Retrieval

Retrieving a fixed number of memory entries for every query is not optimal since some queries might not have relevant memory entries, while there might be many similar entries for other queries.

Prior work (Taguchi et al., 2025;Xu et al., 2025c) in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses the trade-off between missing information with too small k and adding redundancy with too large k, where k is the number of retrieved documents. These methods dynamically decide the number k and show that the optimal amount of retrieved context varies across queries. Adaptive-k (Taguchi et al., 2025) selects "k" as the largest adjacent similarity-score gap.

Our Dynamic "n" approach has four main steps illustrated by the Algorithm 1. The first two steps are calculating the cosine similarity values between the query and memory entries and sorting them in descending order. The third step calculates a first-order derivative estimate of sorted similarities based on a sliding window approach where x is an array of sorted similarities, and R is considered as the "radius" of the derivative estimate. The final step is finding the peaks, i.e., sudden drops in similarity, ideally showing a class boundary. The peak corresponds to our "n" value for Dynamic "n" retrieval. The entire process is inspired by the concept of finding "knees" for designing systems (Satopaa et al., 2011). The find_peaks * function from the SciPy library is utilized for peak finding. Figure 4 illustrates an example. The blue line shows the sorted similarity values, while the red line shows the first derivative estimation. As observed, the locations where there are local maxima, i.e., a peak, correspond to locations with a sudden drop in similarity. Dynamic "n" retrieval has three parameters, namely R, prominence, and the peak number. R is a smoothing parameter, and larger R values result in smoother derivative estimates. Prominence is a parameter of the find_peaks function to filter important peaks based on comparison of neighboring values. The peak number is simply which peak to select. Similarity curves can be noisy, have multiple knees and multi-step drops rather than huge gaps. We hypothesize that finding peaks based on the derivative estimate rather than raw similarity values results in a more robust approach than Adaptivek. Dynamic "n" robustly finds points of change or cluster boundaries on noisy similarity curves, while Adaptive-k finds the biggest drop and works well only when the curve has one clean knee.

sections.heading: Memory Extraction Module
sections.text:
The agent needs to apply experience to the current task based on the user feedback and the context. An important observation from our experiments is that agents struggle to effectively learn from retrieved negative experiences when they are presented as raw execution traces. We hypothesize this is because the agent must simultaneously understand what went wrong in the past example while solving the current task. To make the agent's work easier, a "Memory Extraction" module is proposed. It reflects on the context and user feedback to understand what was wrong. For wrong executions, the reflection/critique is added to the memory instead of the raw context, which might be too complicated and contain irrelevant parts. Doing the reflection as a separate step helps the agent focus only on the current task and learn from its mistakes.

The memory extraction module is an LLM E that takes the following as input: (1) current query q, (2) set of available tools T = {t 1 , t 2 , . . . , t m }, (3) agent's response (actions) a = {a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a n } including tool calls, (4) environment feedback e including tool responses, (5) user feedback f ∈ {0, 1}, and (6) retrieved semantically similar memory entries M ′ ⊂ M. The module outputs a reflection/critique r = E(q, T , a, e, f, M ′ ).

Query: Was total visits more than 21 at any time in the last 1 weeks ? If so , please plot it as a line chart Answer (Tool Calls): [' analytics . total_visits_count . func ( time_min ="2023 -11 -23" , time_max ="2023 -11 -30") ' , ' analytics . create_plot . func ( time_min ="2023 -11 -23" , time_max ="2023 -11 -30" , value_to_plot =" total_visits ", plot_type =" line ") '] User Feedback: Incorrect Reflection: The agent created the line chart despite the condition not being met . The agent concluded correctly that the total visits did not exceed 21 at any point ( the highest was 19 visits on 2023 -11 -28) , but then proceeded to create the line chart anyway . This contradicts the original instruction which specified to plot the data ONLY IF visits exceeded 21. Using retrieved memory entries that are semantically similar to the current user query is important. The main use case for general-purpose tool use is having different queries with common mistakes, which are only sometimes detected by the memory extractor. A similar entry with a correct reflection could help the memory extractor produce a correct critique. For personalized tool use, memory extractor is slightly different. Semantically similar memory entries are used to find user patterns and preferences. The memory extraction module is used to extract high-level user preferences, such as "User prefers tools under AP I_X".

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: Memory can be applied to multiple problem settings in tool-using agents. Our experiments focus on two main tasks: (1) general-purpose tool use and (2) personalization. Three benchmarks, Work-Bench (Styles et al., 2024), NESTFUL (Basu et al., 2024), and PEToolBench (Xu et al., 2025a), were used for evaluation. WorkBench and NESTFUL are general-purpose tool use benchmarks, while PEToolBench is a personalized tool orchestration benchmark.

sections.heading: Benchmarks
sections.text:
WorkBench is an outcome-centric tool use benchmark that evaluates agents on workplace tasks such as sending emails and scheduling meetings. It includes five databases and 27 tools. WorkBench tasks are from different domains like Analytics, Calendar, etc. The evaluation metric is accuracy, which is defined as the percentage of tasks where the outcome from the agent's actions matches the expected outcome. The correct outcome means the correct changes in the database values.

WorkBench queries were created based on predefined templates such as 'Delete an email from person X' or 'Schedule a meeting with person Y'. There are 10 queries per template. Since the benchmark has no train-test split, one query from each template is used to populate the memory. This ensures that there is at least one directly relevant memory entry for each test query. This setup is used to show the advantages of using the memory. The test set consists of 108 Analytics, 99 Calendar, 72 CRM, 81 Email, and 189 Multi-domain tasks.

NESTFUL benchmark evaluates LLMs on nested sequences of tool calls, where the output of one tool call is used as input for the next tool call. It includes 1891 test queries based on MathQA (Amini et al., 2019) and StarCoder2-Instruct (Wei et al., 2024) benchmarks. The first 500 tasks are used as test set while the next 500 tasks are used to populate the memory. The benchmark uses five evaluation metrics, which are F1 scores for tool and parameter generation, Partial Sequence Matching, Full Sequence Matching, and Win Rate. Partial Sequence Matching measures how many predicted APIs with their argument-value pairs match the gold API sequence, Full Sequence Matching evaluates whether the model produces the exact full sequence, and Win Rate assesses whether the predicted APIs lead to the gold answer when executed. PEToolBench is a personalized tool orchestration benchmark. Each query comes with an instruction history consisting of 80-100 past user queries, where each past query includes a binary rating (1 for correct/desired execution, 0 otherwise). For our experiments, this instruction history forms the memory, where each memory entry consists of a past query, its corresponding tool call, and binary user feedback. Test queries are designed such that the agent must rely on user preferences from memory for correct tool execution. A subset of 591 queries is used as the test set after filtering the queries with sufficiently long instruction histories (at least 80 past queries). This makes sure that the agent needs a memory rather than using the full history in context. The benchmark uses two evaluation metrics: Tool Accuracy, which evaluates the model's ability to call the appropriate tool based on user preferences, and Parameter Accuracy, which assesses whether the model generates the correct parameters.

sections.heading: Experiment Results
sections.text: This section presents the main experiments with details, ablation studies demonstrating the contribution of individual MemToolAgent parts, and a cost analysis.

sections.heading: Experiment Settings
sections.text: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Anthropic, 2024) is used for PEToolBench results while NESTFUL and Work-Bench experiments use Claude 3.7 Sonnet (Anthropic, 2025). Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025b) embedding model is used for memory retrieval. All experimental results are based on a single run. Dynamic "n" retrieval hyperparameters are manually tuned. R is set to 10 and prominence is set to 10 -5 . Empirically, using the second peak for PEToolBench performs better while the first peak is the optimal choice for WorkBench and NEST-FUL.

sections.heading: Hard Preference Guiding and Simple Ranking for PEToolBench
sections.text:
Table 4 demonstrates the effectiveness of simple ranker and Hard Preference Guiding ideas through ablation studies. The original approach for PETool-Bench provides the agent with the entire instruction history, which is not optimal, as irrelevant queries can make the task more challenging. Embeddingbased Retrieval_v1 improves this by retrieving only the top-10 semantically similar queries from memory. Retrieval_v2 builds on v1 by introducing a simple ranker that separates memory entries by rating (1 vs. 0) in the system prompt to emphasize user preferences. This is a small modification for personalization tasks. Although it substantially increases the tool accuracy, there is a decrease in parameter accuracy. This is due to binary feedback, which only provides correct/incorrect information.

Negative feedback causes the agent to consider correct parameters as incorrect, as the tool itself can be incorrect even with correct parameters.

Error analysis revealed cases where the agent selected tools despite negative user preferences from the memory. To address this, we introduce an alternative baseline called Hard Preference Guiding which removes tools with a rating of 0 from the system prompt. This is a substitute for the memory extraction module's approach of providing user preferences as soft guidance. It provides a costefficient alternative to the LLM-based memory extraction module, eliminating the need for additional LLM calls during memory addition. Hard Preference Guiding extends MemToolAgent w/o memory extractor and improves Tool Accuracy from 0.72 to 0.84, as shown in Table 4. Although less general than memory extraction, Hard Preference Guiding is effective for scenarios like PEToolBench and could be used as a complementary approach.

sections.heading: Experiments with Different Memory
sections.text: Entry Types start scenario where no queries exist to populate the memory before inference. Given the tool descriptions, an LLM generates synthetic queries, which are then executed and added to the memory. Using synthetic queries improves results compared to the no-memory baseline, except on multi-domain tasks. For multi-domain tasks, it is challenging to generate queries that are both complex enough and sufficiently similar to the test set. Nevertheless, this still demonstrates that synthetic queries can help avoid starting with an empty memory.

sections.heading: Token Usage Analysis
sections.text: Table 5 shows the total number of input and output tokens used by Claude 3.7 Sonnet for 50 NESTFUL test queries. Although MemToolAgent increases the total number of input tokens, the number of output tokens has a much lower increase compared to the Extended Thinking and ReAct baselines. This is an advantage given that output tokens tend to be more expensive and contribute more to the overall response latency.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: MemToolAgent is a memory framework that enhances the tool-using capabilities of LLM agents by using past experiences. The results show significant improvements across multiple benchmarks in both personalized and general-purpose tool use scenarios. The main contributions of the framework include (1) a retrieval mechanism that dynamically determines the number of relevant memory entries to retrieve, (2) a memory extraction module that generates reflections on incorrect executions to help avoid similar mistakes, and (3) an overall effective approach for both general-purpose and personalized tool use based on user and environment feedback.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
Despite the improvements in general-purpose and personalized tool use performance achieved by MemToolAgent, several limitations remain for future work. One limitation is the cold-start problem of memory. Moreover, the benchmarks used contain fewer than 40 tools. However, there are typically more tools in real-life applications. As the number of tools increases, it is more challenging to cover the usage of all tools with memory. This could potentially make the cold-start problem more severe. Our experiments using synthetically generated queries show that even a simple approach can help the cold-start problem.

Another limitation emerges in conversational scenarios with multiple turns. The benchmarks used in our experiments are single-turn. For singleturn tasks, the memory retrieval is done once at the beginning of the conversation. This might not be optimal for multiple-user turn tasks where the agent needs to obtain the necessary information from the user across multiple turns. One possible solution is to extend MemToolAgent to retrieve from memory after each user turn, so that the agent can focus on the sub-task associated with that specific turn. sults demonstrate that extra reasoning alone is not
enough, and the model requires concrete examples
from memory to properly follow the tool calling
format. MemToolAgent demonstrates significant
performance improvements on WorkBench, with
Analytics task accuracy increasing from 18% to
86% and overall accuracy rising from 57% to 85%
compared to the no-memory baseline.
4.2.3 Personalized Tool Orchestration
Experiments
Table 2 shows MemToolAgent's performance com-
pared to state-of-the-art memory architectures A-
MEM and Mem0 on PEToolBench. Due to the cost
of LLM calls for memory addition in these meth-
ods and the MemToolAgent with memory extractor,
the experiments used a 50-query subset consisting
of the first 50 queries from the 591-query test set.
Top-15 embedding-based retrieval was used for
A-MEM and Mem0. MemToolAgent achieves a
Tool Accuracy of 0.82, representing a 17% rela-
tive improvement over A-MEM and Mem0. This
demonstrates that MemToolAgent is more effective
at leveraging memories for selecting the appropri-
ate tool based on user preferences. All methods
perform equally well at generating the appropriate
parameters.
